title: The Sun Fooled NORAD
subtitle: The 1967 Solar Storm That Blinded America's Missile Radars and Nearly Started a War
core_thesis: On May 23, 1967, a colossal solar radio burst blinded all three US BMEWS early-warning radars simultaneously; NORAD read the interference as Soviet jamming and readied nuclear-armed bombers to launch. Forecasters at NORAD's Solar Forecast Center correctly identified the Sun in time, no aircraft launched, and the episode remained classified for nearly 50 years until the 2016 Knipp et al. paper in AGU's Space Weather journal.
counter_intuitive_hook: The United States nearly went to war with the Soviet Union over a weather event — and the person who stopped the war was a weather forecaster.

beats.title: Three Screens Go Dark
beats.caption: May 23, 1967. The three radar sites guarding America from Soviet missiles go dark — all at the same second.
beats.heroLabel: Clear AK · Thule GL · Fylingdales UK
beats.takeawayBullet: BMEWS interference looked exactly like deliberate Soviet jamming.
key_events: Colossal solar radio burst at 0.01-9.0 GHz (largest radio burst of the 20th century)
Radar interference at all three BMEWS sites appeared simultaneously
PAVE PAWS sites (Beale, Cape Cod) not yet operational
beats.visual_direction: Three radome cutouts (Clear, Thule, Fylingdales) enter in stepped stop-motion; radar sweep lines die mid-rotation with 1-bit static tear; red-ribbon date stamp; teletype types site names, each struck through in red as its screen dies.

beats.title: Jamming Means War
beats.caption: In Cold War doctrine, jamming meant one thing: Soviet attack was imminent. Nuclear-armed bombers were moved to ready-to-launch.
beats.takeawayBullet: Documented: aircraft readied, crews scrambled to planes — no bombers launched.
key_events: 1967 doctrine: jamming BMEWS = act of war / prelude to attack
Commanders placed additional forces in 'ready to launch' status
Continuous airborne-alert B-52s through most of the 1960s
Briefing likely reached top officials, possibly President Johnson
beats.visual_direction: Doctrine memo card stamps red 'JAMMING = ACT OF WAR'; B-52 cutout on alert strip (taxi, cut before takeoff — no aircraft launched); 1967 NORAD Cheyenne Mountain photo behind perforated mask; punch-card portal clatters 'ALERT'.

beats.title: The Sun Rolls Out Its Move
beats.caption: Days earlier, a vast sunspot group had rotated onto the Sun. On May 21 and 23 it erupted — flares, then the century's biggest radio burst.
beats.takeawayBullet: 76 flares of importance >=1 counted May 23-27; four major flares on May 23.
key_events: May 18: unusually large sunspot group (McMath region 8818) rotates into view
May 21 and 23: major flare sequence, H-alpha importance up to 3B (Dodson & Hedeman 1969)
May 23: four major flares + colossal radio burst; flare visible to naked eye from New Mexico and Colorado
NORAD Solar Forecast Center bulletin forecasts worldwide geomagnetic storm in 36-48 hours
beats.visual_direction: Carrington-style sunspot drawing slips onto card; SDO X-class flare imagery as modern witness; 1-bit frequency axis 0.01-9.0 GHz draws with red burst spike; 'McMath 8818' typed in; Olivetti CRT shows H-alpha sequence flickering.

beats.title: Half the Sun Has Blown Away
beats.caption: At Ent Air Force Base, Colorado, forecaster Arnold Snyder got the panicked call. His answer: 'Yes — half the sun has blown away.'
beats.heroLabel: Col. Arnold L. Snyder · Solar Forecast Center
beats.takeawayBullet: 4th Weather Wing forecaster's call reached the man who knew the Sun.
key_events: Col. Arnold L. Snyder on duty at NORAD's Solar Forecast Center, Ent AFB, Colorado Springs
4th Weather Wing tropospheric forecaster calls; Snyder: 'Yes, half the sun has blown away'
4th Weather Wing documented at Ent AFB via paper bibliography (4WWM 105-1, April 1, 1966)
Air Weather Service monitored solar flares and fed observations to NORAD forecasters
beats.visual_direction: Ent AFB operations card; 1-bit phone ringer; Snyder quote in oversized typewriter serif with red underline on 'half the sun'; Solar Forecast Center bulletin types live behind (36-48 hour storm forecast); teletype re-print portal as the answer channel.

beats.title: The Jamming Fades
beats.caption: Forecasters confirmed all three radar sites sat in daylight. As the Sun's burst faded, the 'jamming' faded with it. The launch order never came.
beats.takeawayBullet: No aircraft launched; information reached commanders in time, possibly to President Johnson.
key_events: All three BMEWS sites were in sunlight when the burst hit
As solar radio emissions waned, the 'jamming' waned — solar origin confirmed
CME arrived ~40 hours after the flare; major storm May 25-26 (Dst -387 nT, 6 hours at Kp 9)
Radio communications disrupted nearly a week; auroras as far south as New Mexico
beats.visual_direction: Split strip: solar burst curve descending (left) mirrors radar traces normalizing (right) in lockstep — the correlation is the punchline; stamp flips JAMMING to SOLAR; three site cards flip to green sweep; B-52 taxis backward off strip.

assets.name: BMEWS radar beam diagram (signal normalization visual)

beats.title: Secret for 50 Years
beats.caption: The near-war stayed secret for half a century — until 2016, when a declassified study named the culprit: the May 1967 Great Storm.
beats.takeawayBullet: Paper: 'The May 1967 Great Storm and Radio Disruption Event: Extreme Space Weather and Extraordinary Responses.'
key_events: Knipp et al., Space Weather 14(9):614-633, DOI 10.1002/2016SW001423, published online Sept 5, 2016
Authors include Knipp + retirees of USAF Air Weather Service (Ramsay, Beard, Boright) and AF Research Lab (Shea, Smart)
Knipp: 'things were going horribly wrong, and then something goes commendably right'
Outcome: more formal DoD support for current-day space weather forecasting
beats.visual_direction: CLASSIFIED folder gets red DECLASSIFIED stamp; 2016 paper title types line by line; Knipp quote card; punch-card portal feeds the 1966 4th Weather Wing manual citation.

beats.title: The Sun Is Still Shooting
beats.caption: Quebec went dark in 1989. Earth missed a Carrington-class blast by days in 2012. We just passed solar maximum. The Sun never demobilized.
beats.takeawayBullet: March 13, 1989: Hydro-Quebec grid collapsed in 90 seconds, 6 million people, ~9 hours.
key_events: March 13, 1989: Hydro-Quebec blackout, 90 seconds to collapse, 6 million people, ~9 hours
July 23, 2012: Carrington-class CME crossed Earth's orbit, hit STEREO-A; ~9 days earlier and it would have hit Earth
Solar Cycle 25 maximum officially announced Oct 15, 2024 by NASA/NOAA; maximum phase continues into 2025-2026
'The day the sun declared war' is modern 2016-era editorial framing, not a 1967 headline
beats.visual_direction: Sunspot-cycle chart animates 1610-present with cycle 20 peak lit for 1967; ISS aurora behind dithered mask; 1989 grid-collapse and 2012 near-miss cards stamp in sequence; end card 'NORAD's radars listen. So does the Sun.' CTA in bottom caption zone only.

solar_event.sunspot_region: McMath plage region 8818, rotated into view May 18, 1967 (AGU press release; Space.com)
solar_event.flare_sequence: Major flares May 21 and May 23, 1967, H-alpha importance up to 3B (Dodson & Hedeman 1969, Solar Physics)
solar_event.radio_burst: Colossal solar radio burst 0.01-9.0 GHz, largest of the 20th century, May 23, 1967 (Knipp et al. 2016 abstract)
solar_event.flare_count: 76 flares of importance >=1 during May 23-27 (Knipp et al. 2016)
solar_event.geomagnetic_storm: May 25-26, 1967: Dst -387 nT, 6 hours at Kp 9, double sudden commencement 1019/1235 UT May 25; largest solar proton event on record followed
solar_event.disruption_duration: Radio communications disrupted nearly a week; auroras as far south as New Mexico
solar_event.classification_note: Modern M/X-class system did not exist in 1967; exact modern class not assigned in literature (corrected claim)
